overview.title: 📖 Overview: Closing Chapter Four, Opening Chapter Five
overview.subtitle: Temurah 24a–24b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Rabbi Hoshaya's ruling — that of two sin offerings designated as a mutual guarantee, atoning with one leaves the other to graze rather than die — is tested against the Rabbis, Rabbi Shimon, and finally pinned specifically to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's own distinction between 'replacing a loss' and merely 'guaranteeing.' A related baraita distinguishing when an animal was lost (at designation vs. at atonement) is corrected by Rav Pappa's a fortiori logic. A digression on flaying disqualified or firstborn animals 'from the feet' uncovers three separate prohibitions with three distinct rationales. Chapter Four closes and Chapter Five opens with a new mishna on lawful artifice: designating an unborn fetus for a different offering (based on its eventual sex) to redirect it away from automatic firstborn status — along with the Gemara's discussion of whether one may even blemish such a fetus before it is born.

slides.title: 🐐 Two Sin Offerings as a Guarantee — Whose View Is This?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Hoshaya's ruling tested against three candidate opinions

lines.speaker: Rabbi Hoshaya
lines.text: One who designates TWO sin offerings as mutual insurance atones with either one; the other simply grazes (not dies).

lines.speaker: Test: the Rabbis?
lines.text: Redundant — if even a true REPLACEMENT-for-loss isn't treated as lost by the Rabbis, obviously a mere guarantee isn't either.

lines.speaker: Test: Rabbi Shimon?
lines.text: Contradicted — Rabbi Shimon says ALL FIVE sin-offering-dies cases apply unconditionally, with no guarantee exception.

lines.speaker: Conclusion: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
lines.text: This must be Rebbi's own view: his 'dies' ruling applies ONLY when replacing something already lost — never to money or animals set aside merely as advance insurance.

callout.label: A near-miss test:
callout.text: Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon's own ruling (that a sold, blemished sin offering still 'dies in status' if the replacement is sacrificed first) initially looks like Rebbi's view extended too far — but is reattributed to his father Rabbi Shimon's unconditional position instead.

slides.title: ⏱️ Correcting a Baraita on Timing
slides.subtitle: Rav Shimi bar Ziri's version vs. Rav Pappa's logical fix

nodes.content: 📜 First version: lost at DESIGNATION (before atonement) → Rebbi: dies; Rabbis: grazes. Lost at ATONEMENT → Rabbis: dies; Rebbi: grazes

❓ Rav Pappa's objection: if the Rabbis are lenient (grazes) even for the MORE severe case (lost at designation), how could they be STRICT (dies) for the LESS severe case (lost at atonement)? That's backwards!
✅ Corrected version: lost at designation → Rebbi: dies; Rabbis: grazes (as before). Lost at atonement → EVERYONE agrees: dies

callout.label: The logical principle used:
callout.text: A kal vachomer (a fortiori inference): whatever the lenient position permits in the harder case must also be permitted in the easier case — any contradiction to that pattern signals a transmission error.

slides.title: 🦶 Why Flaying 'From the Feet' Is Sometimes Forbidden
slides.subtitle: Three separate cases, three separate rationales

boxes.title: On a Festival (all agree)
items: Forbidden simply because it's needless extra EFFORT unfit for the day
Applies to any animal, sacred or not

boxes.title: A Firstborn — Beit Shammai
items: A blemished firstborn retains real sanctity (an Israelite can't even share it with a priest)
So flaying it 'from the feet' (a labor-like act) is forbidden
Limited to firstborn — sanctified from birth itself

boxes.title: Disqualified Consecrated Animals — R' Elazar b'R' Shimon
items: Even after redemption, sanctity can persist strongly enough to reach the money — as when a sold sin offering 'dies in status'
Alternative reasons offered: it LOOKS like performing labor with a sacred animal (Eretz Yisrael sages); or a decree against DELAYING slaughter to find a hide-buyer, risking illicit flock-raising

callout.label: Why the sources can't simply merge:
callout.text: Beit Shammai's firstborn-specific reasoning (sanctified 'from the womb') doesn't obviously extend to redeemed disqualified animals, and vice versa — each case needs its own tanna and its own logic.

slides.title: 🐄 New Mishna: Artifice to Avoid Firstborn Status
slides.subtitle: Redirecting a fetus's future sanctity before it's even born
rows: 'If male, a burnt offering' — born male
'If female, a peace offering' — born female
Gave birth to one male AND one female
Male → burnt offering; female → peace offering
One sacrificed as a burnt offering; the other SOLD to someone else who needs one — its sale proceeds are non-sacred
Gave birth to a tumtum or hermaphrodite (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel)
No sanctity takes hold on them at all

callout.label: Why this works:
callout.text: By designating the fetus's sanctity BEFORE birth based on a condition (its eventual sex), the owner redirects it entirely away from automatic firstborn status — a lawful use of foresight, not deception.

slides.title: 🤰 May One Blemish the Fetus Before It's Born?
slides.subtitle: Rav Yehuda's ruling, limited carefully to the present era

nodes.content: ❓ Rav Yehuda: it's permitted to blemish a firstborn fetus before it emerges — it has no sanctity yet
⚠️ Objection: but the mishna itself only allows REDIRECTING sanctity (to a burnt/peace offering), not ABOLISHING it via blemish — doesn't that prove blemishing beforehand is forbidden?

💬 Rav Yehuda clarifies: that mishna describes Temple times, when sacrifice is possible; my ruling is for TODAY, when firstborns can't be sacrificed anyway — so pre-emptive blemishing is the only way to make it usable at all

✅ Even so: why not fear that blemishing right as 'most of the head' emerges (the exact moment sanctity begins) might strike an ALREADY-sacred animal? Answer: this concern doesn't override the greater risk of violating shearing/labor prohibitions while waiting for a natural blemish

callout.label: Practical logic:
callout.text: Since today's firstborn can only be eaten once blemished anyway, allowing an early blemish avoids the greater risk of accidentally working or shearing it during a long wait.

summary.principle: Only genuine replacement-for-loss (never mere guarantee-insurance) triggers Rebbi's stringent 'dies' rule, disqualified animals may not be flayed 'from the feet' for several independent reasons, and lawful artifice can redirect an unborn fetus's sanctity away from automatic firstborn status — including, nowadays, by blemishing it before birth.

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Torah law distinguishes sharply between replacing a genuine loss and merely hedging in advance

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's conclusion, whose opinion does Rabbi Hoshaya's ruling (two sin offerings as a guarantee — the unused one grazes) actually represent?
o: The Rabbis, since it's obviously redundant for them
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi (Rebbi), whose stringent 'dies' rule applies only to true replacement-for-loss, not mere guarantee-insurance
Rabbi Shimon, who treats all cases unconditionally
No named authority — it stands alone
quiz.e: After testing against the Rabbis (redundant) and Rabbi Shimon (contradicted, since he applies 'dies' unconditionally), the Gemara concludes Rabbi Hoshaya represents Rebbi's own distinction between genuine loss-replacement and mere guarantee.

quiz.q: What logical tool does Rav Pappa use to correct Rav Shimi bar Ziri's baraita about timing (lost at designation vs. lost at atonement)?
o: A verbal analogy (gezeirah shava)
An a fortiori inference (kal vachomer) — the lenient position in a harder case must also apply in an easier case
A tradition from Sinai
A simple textual emendation with no logical basis
quiz.e: Rav Pappa uses a kal vachomer: since the Rabbis are lenient (grazes) even in the more severe 'lost at designation' case, they cannot be strict (dies) in the less severe 'lost at atonement' case — forcing a correction to unanimous agreement there.

quiz.q: According to Beit Shammai, why is it forbidden to flay a firstborn animal 'from the feet,' even when it is blemished?
o: Because it's always forbidden to slaughter any animal on any day
Because a blemished firstborn retains real sanctity (an Israelite may not even share it with a priest), so labor-like handling remains forbidden
Because firstborns can never be blemished
Because only priests may touch firstborn animals
quiz.e: Beit Shammai hold that a firstborn's sanctity persists even after it becomes blemished, evidenced by their ruling that an Israelite cannot share ownership of it with a priest — making labor-like flaying still prohibited.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what happens if a designated fetus is born as TWO males (with 'if male, a burnt offering' having been declared)?
o: Both are sacrificed as burnt offerings
One is sacrificed as a burnt offering; the other is sold to someone else who needs a burnt offering, and its sale proceeds are non-sacred
Both are left to die
Neither is sacrificed
quiz.e: Since only the original condition ('if male') can apply to one specific offering, one male is sacrificed as a burnt offering while the second is sold to another owner in need of one, with the money becoming non-sacred.

quiz.q: According to Rav Yehuda, when is it permitted to inflict a blemish on a firstborn fetus before it is born?
o: Only when the Temple stands
Only nowadays, when the Temple does not stand and firstborns cannot be sacrificed regardless
Never, under any circumstances
Only if the mother is also blemished
quiz.e: Rav Yehuda limits his permissive ruling to the present era without a Temple, where a firstborn can only ever be eaten once blemished anyway — distinguishing it from Temple times, when the mishna's designation-based artifice (not blemishing) is required instead.
